label: HSC 12 Differentiation 1.1.3 SolvedEx.6
reason: flawed: Balbharati 12 Maths Part 2 Ch 1, Ex. 6 (p. 11) prints x = pi/3; its hint basket and solution give sqrt 3, the value at pi/6
solution:
**Note:** As printed, the last blank asks for the value at \(x = \frac{\pi}{3}\), where \(\cot\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\). The book's hint basket and its answer give \(\sqrt{3}\), which is the value at \(x = \frac{\pi}{6}\). The answers shown follow the book.

[Textbook misprint: the activity asks for the derivative at \(x=\frac{\pi}{3}\), where \(\cot\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) — but the hint basket offers only \(\sqrt{3}\), and the book's own solution ends with \(\sqrt{3}\). The evaluation point should read \(x=\frac{\pi}{6}\), for which \(\cot\frac{\pi}{6}=\sqrt{3}\).]

\(\sin(\log x)\), \(\log(\sin x)\), \(\cos x\), \(\frac{1}{x}\), \(f'[g(x)] \cdot g'(x)\), \(\frac{\cos(\log x)}{x}\), \(1\), \(g'[f(x)] \cdot f'(x)\), \(\cot x\), \(\sqrt{3}\).

label: HSC 12 Trigonometric Functions Misc I Q.19
reason: flawed: Balbharati 12 Maths Part 1 Ch 3 Misc I Q19: no printed option is the full solution set n pi/3; book key (b) n pi/6
solution:
**Note:** As printed, no option is exactly the solution set: the equation holds when \(\theta = \frac{n\pi}{3}\). The answer shown follows the book's key, \(\frac{n\pi}{6}\), which contains every solution but also values where \(\tan 3\theta\) is undefined.

[Textbook defect: the complete solution set is \(\theta=\dfrac{n\pi}{3}\), which is not among the four printed alternatives. The official key marks \(\dfrac{n\pi}{6}\), retained here to match the board: it contains the whole solution set as its even-\(n\) members, but also contains values such as \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\) at which \(\tan 3\theta\) is undefined.]

Since \(3\theta=\theta+2\theta\), \(\tan 3\theta=\dfrac{\tan\theta+\tan 2\theta}{1-\tan\theta\tan 2\theta}\), that is \(\tan\theta+\tan 2\theta=\tan 3\theta\left(1-\tan\theta\tan 2\theta\right)\).

Substituting this in the given equation:

\(\tan 3\theta\left(1-\tan\theta\tan 2\theta\right)+\tan 3\theta=\tan\theta\tan 2\theta\tan 3\theta\)

\(\Rightarrow\ 2\tan 3\theta\left(1-\tan\theta\tan 2\theta\right)=0\).

The factor \(1-\tan\theta\tan 2\theta\) vanishes exactly where \(\tan 3\theta\) is undefined, so it yields no solution of the given equation. Hence \(\tan 3\theta=0\), i.e. \(3\theta=n\pi\), giving \(\theta=\dfrac{n\pi}{3}\).

Following the official key, (B).

label: HSC 12 Trigonometric Functions Misc II Q.12
reason: flawed: Balbharati 12 Maths Part 1 Ch 3 Misc II Q12 prints the half-angle cotangents
solution:
**Note:** As printed, the statement does not hold: when \(a^2, b^2, c^2\) are in A.P., it is \(\cot A, \cot B, \cot C\) that are in A.P., not the half-angle cotangents. The proof below shows the true result.

[Textbook note: As printed, with the HALF-angle cotangents \(\cot\frac{A}{2},\cot\frac{B}{2},\cot\frac{C}{2}\), the result does not hold when \(a^2,b^2,c^2\) are in A.P. (those half-angle cotangents are in A.P. precisely when \(a,b,c\) are in A.P.). The standard, correct result for the hypothesis \(a^2,b^2,c^2\) in A.P. is that \(\cot A,\cot B,\cot C\) are in A.P., proved below.]

By the cosine and sine rules,
\(\cot A=\dfrac{\cos A}{\sin A}=\dfrac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}\cdot\dfrac{2R}{a}=\dfrac{R(b^2+c^2-a^2)}{abc}\).
Similarly \(\cot B=\dfrac{R(a^2+c^2-b^2)}{abc}\) and \(\cot C=\dfrac{R(a^2+b^2-c^2)}{abc}\).
Given \(a^2,b^2,c^2\) in A.P., we have \(a^2+c^2=2b^2\).
Now \(\cot A+\cot C=\dfrac{R}{abc}\big[(b^2+c^2-a^2)+(a^2+b^2-c^2)\big]=\dfrac{R}{abc}(2b^2)\).
Also \(2\cot B=\dfrac{2R}{abc}(a^2+c^2-b^2)=\dfrac{2R}{abc}(2b^2-b^2)=\dfrac{R}{abc}(2b^2)\).
\(\therefore \cot A+\cot C=2\cot B\), i.e. \(\cot A,\cot B,\cot C\) are in A.P. Hence proved.

label: HSC 12 Physics Thermodynamics Solved Ex.4.2
reason: flawed: Balbharati 12 Physics Ch 4 Example 4.2 states no initial volume; its own solution takes the change in volume as 0.5
solution:
**Note:** The book's example does not state the initial volume. Its solution takes the change in volume as \(0.5\ \text{m}^3\) (an initial volume of \(0.5\ \text{m}^3\)), and the working below follows it.

Given: Pressure of one atmosphere \(p = 1.01 \times 10^{5}\) Pa, change in volume \((V_{f} - V_{i}) = 0.5\).

\(W = p (V_{f} - V_{i}) = 1.01 \times 10^{5} (+0.5)\)

\(= 0.505 \times 10^{5} = 5.05 \times 10^{4}\) J

Is this work done on the gas or by the gas? How do you know this?

label: HSC 12 Physics Thermodynamics PYQ 2017 Q.1(i)
reason: flawed: Maharashtra HSC board paper 2017 (chapterwise compilation) Q1(i): option (d) printed 11.4%, the working gives 11.1%
solution:
**Note:** As printed, no option is exact: the volume rises by \(11.1\%\), and option (D) prints \(11.4\%\). The answer shown is (D), the nearest option.

**(D)** the volume increases

**Data:** the process is isothermal; the pressure decreases by \(10\%\), so \(p_{f} = 0.9\,p_{i}\).

**Relation.** For a fixed mass of an ideal gas at constant temperature, Boyle's law gives \(pV = \) constant, i.e.

\(p_{i}V_{i} = p_{f}V_{f}\)

**Final volume.**

\(V_{f} = \dfrac{p_{i}V_{i}}{p_{f}} = \dfrac{p_{i}V_{i}}{0.9\,p_{i}} = \dfrac{V_{i}}{0.9} = 1.111\,V_{i}\)

**Percentage change in volume.**

\(\dfrac{V_{f} - V_{i}}{V_{i}} \times 100 = (1.111 - 1) \times 100 = 11.1\%\)

**Check.** \(p_{f}V_{f} = (0.9\,p_{i})(1.111\,V_{i}) = 1.000\,p_{i}V_{i}\), so the product \(pV\) is unchanged, as an isothermal change requires. The rise is not \(10\%\): restoring the product after the pressure has fallen to \(0.9\,p_{i}\) needs the volume multiplied by \(\dfrac{1}{0.9}\), not by \(1.1\).

\(\therefore\) the volume increases by about \(11\%\).

[The printed option is wrong by a rounding slip, and the board's paper is the source: J-531 prints 'increase by 11.4%'. Boyle's law gives \(V_{f}/V_{i} = 1/0.9\), an increase of \(11.11\%\), and no self-consistent reading of the stem returns 11.4% (that would need a 10.23% fall in pressure, not 10%). The option is keyed on that basis, since it is the only alternative of the right size; the exact figure is 11.11%.]

label: HSC 12 Physics EMI PYQ 2023 Q.28(ii)
reason: flawed: Maharashtra HSC board paper 2023 (chapterwise compilation) Q28(ii): the Earth's horizontal field B_H is not given
solution:
**Note:** As printed, this cannot be answered in numbers: the emf depends on the Earth's horizontal magnetic field \(B_H\), which the paper does not give. The answer below is left in terms of \(B_H\).

**Speed with which the wire reaches the ground.** The wire is released from rest and falls freely through \(h = 15\) m, so with \(g = 10\ \text{m/s}^{2}\),

\(\mathrm{v}^{2} = u^{2} + 2gh = 0 + 2(10)(15) = 300\)

\(\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{300} = 17.32\) m/s

**Average speed over the fall.** The acceleration is uniform, so the average speed is the mean of the initial and final speeds:

\(\mathrm{v}_{\text{av}} = \dfrac{0 + 17.32}{2} = 8.66\) m/s

**Average emf induced.** The wire is supported along the east-west direction and falls vertically, so the wire, its velocity and the **horizontal** component \(B_{H}\) of the Earth's magnetic field (which points north) are mutually perpendicular. The average motional emf is therefore

\(e_{\text{av}} = B_{H}\,l\,\mathrm{v}_{\text{av}}\)

with \(l = 5\) m,

\(\therefore e_{\text{av}} = B_{H} \times 5 \times 8.66 = 43.3\,B_{H}\) volt

No value of \(B_{H}\) is supplied — neither in the question nor among the physical constants printed with the paper — so the emf cannot be reduced to a number and must be left in this form. Were \(B_{H}\) taken as \(0.3 \times 10^{-4}\) T, a value of the order of the Earth's horizontal field, this would give \(43.3 \times 0.3 \times 10^{-4} = 1.30 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{V} \approx 1.3\) mV; that figure rests on a datum the question does not give and is offered only to show the size of the quantity.

Check on the structure of the answer: using the average speed is what makes the emf an **average** one. The instantaneous emf just before impact would be \(B_{H}(5)(17.32) = 86.6\,B_{H}\) volt, twice as large, since the wire is then moving at twice its average speed.

[Board defect: the question cannot be evaluated as a number. A motional e.m.f. needs the value of the Earth's magnetic field, and the paper gives none - checked against the printed February 2023 paper, whose own Physical Constants block on page 1 lists only \(h\), \(c\), \(\pi\), \(g\), \(\varepsilon_{0}\) and \(\mu_{0}\). The stem here is exactly as printed and has not been repaired. The answer is therefore left in terms of \(B_{H}\); substitute the value your board supplies.]

label: HSC 12 Physics Magnetic Fields Ex Q.1(iii)
reason: flawed: Balbharati 12 Physics Ch 10 Ex Q1(iii) prints option (B) as 'positive x axis'; the book prints no MCQ key
solution:
**Note:** As printed, no option is correct: the proton bends towards the positive \(y\) axis. Option (B), printed "bending towards positive \(x\) axis", is evidently meant to read positive \(y\) axis, and the answer shown follows that reading.

[Textbook misprint: option (B) is printed as "It will move along a curved path, bending towards positive \(x\) axis". As printed, no option is correct — a particle already travelling along the positive \(x\) axis cannot bend towards it — while the derivation above gives a deflection towards the positive \(y\) axis. Read alongside option (C), which names the negative \(y\) axis, option (B) is a misprint for "positive \(y\) axis", and it is keyed here on that reading. The book prints no MCQ key anywhere, so this is an adjudication of the printed options rather than a disagreement with a printed key.]

Take \(\hat{x}\) along the axis, \(\hat{y}\) upward in the plane of the page and \(\hat{z}\) out of the page. The proton has \(\vec{v} = v\hat{x}\); the field is directed into the paper, so \(\vec{B} = -B\hat{z}\).

\(\vec{F} = q\,\vec{v}\times\vec{B} = q(v\hat{x})\times(-B\hat{z}) = -qvB\,(\hat{x}\times\hat{z}) = -qvB(-\hat{y}) = +qvB\,\hat{y}\)

The force on the (positively charged) proton is therefore along the **positive \(y\)** direction. It stays perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\) at every instant, so the proton turns along a circular arc at constant speed, curving **upward, towards the positive \(y\) axis**.

The three alternatives fail outright. Continuing along the positive \(x\) axis requires zero force, but \(\vec{v}\perp\vec{B}\) gives the maximum possible magnetic force. Bending towards the negative \(y\) axis has the deflection the wrong way round — that is the path of a negative charge, or of a proton in a field directed out of the page. A sinusoidal path needs a restoring force that reverses sign along the path, whereas a uniform magnetic field of constant magnitude produces a constant-speed circular arc.

label: HSC 12 Physics KTG PYQ June 2025 Q.1(ix)
reason: flawed: Maharashtra HSC board paper June 2025 (J-339) Q1(ix): every option printed in degrees C
solution:
**Note:** As printed, the options are in the wrong unit: the working gives an initial temperature of \(250\ \text{K}\) (that is, \(-23^\circ\text{C}\)), but every option is in \(^\circ\text{C}\). The answer shown is (B), the option carrying 250.

**(B)** 250°C

The gas is in a closed vessel, so the volume is constant and Gay-Lussac's law applies:

\(\dfrac{P}{T} = \text{constant}\), hence \(\dfrac{\Delta P}{P} = \dfrac{\Delta T}{T}\)

Here the pressure rises by 0.4 per cent for a rise of \(1^{\circ}\text{C}\), so \(\dfrac{\Delta P}{P} = 0.004\) and \(\Delta T = 1\).

\(0.004 = \dfrac{1}{T}\)

\(T = \dfrac{1}{0.004} = 250\)

\(\therefore\) the initial temperature is \(250\), the numeral that option (b) carries.

It is worth being exact about what the working gives: since \(P \propto T\) holds only for **absolute** temperature, the \(250\) here is in kelvin, that is \(-23^{\circ}\text{C}\). All four options are printed in degree Celsius, so the printed unit does not match the physics; the numeral, however, is uniquely determined and only option (b) carries it.

label: HSC 12 Chemistry Solutions Ex Q.2(iv)
reason: flawed: Balbharati 12 Chemistry Ch 2 Ex Q2(iv) prints a freezing point of -4.3 C
solution:
**Note:** As printed, the freezing point \(-4.3^\circ\mathrm{C}\) gives \(i = 23.1\), which is impossible for \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\) (at most 3). The book evidently means \(-0.43^\circ\mathrm{C}\), which gives \(i = 2.31\). The working below follows the printed value.

[Textbook misprint: the printed freezing point \(-4.3^\circ\mathrm{C}\) gives \(i = 4.3/(1.86 \times 0.1) = 23.1\), which is impossible, since \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\) yields at most 3 particles per formula unit. A freezing point of \(-0.43^\circ\mathrm{C}\) gives the admissible \(i = 2.31\), so the decimal point appears to be misplaced. The question is worked below exactly as printed.]

The van't Hoff factor is the ratio of the observed freezing point depression to the value expected for a nonelectrolyte of the same concentration:

\(i = \dfrac{(\Delta T_f)}{(\Delta T_f)_0} = \dfrac{\Delta T_f}{K_f m}\)

Working with the data exactly as printed:

\(\Delta T_f = 0^\circ\mathrm{C} - (-4.3^\circ\mathrm{C}) = 4.3\ \mathrm{K}\)

\((\Delta T_f)_0 = K_f m = 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}} \times 0.1\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}} = 0.186\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(i = \dfrac{4.3\ \mathrm{K}}{0.186\ \mathrm{K}} = 23.1\)

This value is not physically possible. \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\) dissociates as \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{K^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\), giving at most 3 particles per formula unit, so \(i\) cannot exceed 3. A freezing point of \(-0.43^\circ\mathrm{C}\) would give

\(i = \dfrac{0.43\ \mathrm{K}}{0.186\ \mathrm{K}} = 2.31\)

which is an admissible value (below the ideal 3, as expected once ion pairing is allowed for). The printed freezing point therefore appears to carry a misplaced decimal point.
